title: How Ancient DNA Is Rewriting Human History

slides.heading: How Ancient DNA Is Rewriting Human History
slides.body: What bones from 40,000 years ago reveal about who we really are

slides.heading: The Paleogenomics Revolution
slides.body: Scientists can now extract and sequence DNA from ancient bones, teeth, and even cave sediments. Since 2010, researchers have decoded thousands of ancient human genomes — transforming what we know about our past.

slides.heading: We All Carry Neanderthal DNA
slides.body: Modern humans outside Africa carry 1–4% Neanderthal DNA. Ancient DNA proved this interbreeding happened when Homo sapiens migrated out of Africa around 60,000 years ago. Some Neanderthal genes affect our immune system and even our COVID-19 risk.

slides.heading: The Denisovans: A Ghost Species Revealed
slides.body: A tiny finger bone from Siberia's Denisova Cave revealed an entirely unknown human species in 2010. Denisovans interbred with our ancestors too — modern Tibetans carry Denisovan gene variants that help them survive high altitudes.

slides.heading: Europe's Dramatic Population Replacements
slides.body: Ancient DNA shows Europe was not settled gradually. Around 5,000 years ago, steppe pastoralists from the Eurasian grasslands swept in and replaced up to 90% of Western Europe's farmers. Modern Europeans are largely descended from this Bronze Age migration.

slides.heading: Rewriting the Story of the Americas
slides.body: DNA from ancient skeletons has revealed at least three separate waves of migration into the Americas. One mysterious group, related to Amazonian peoples, left genetic traces in ancient Alaskans — suggesting a far more complex settlement than once thought.

slides.heading: Ancient Plagues and Pandemics
slides.body: Ancient DNA has identified plague (Yersinia pestis) in 5,000-year-old skeletons, predating written records by millennia. These early strains may have triggered massive population collapses in Neolithic Europe long before the Black Death.

slides.heading: The Limits of Skin, Hair, and Eye Color
slides.body: We can now predict traits from ancient DNA. Cheddar Man, a 10,000-year-old British skeleton, had dark skin and blue eyes — challenging assumptions that pale skin was ancient in Europe. Lighter skin evolved much more recently than expected.

slides.heading: Ethics and Indigenous Communities
slides.body: Ancient DNA research raises serious ethical questions. Many indigenous communities object to destructive sampling of ancestral remains without consent. Researchers now increasingly work in partnership with descendant communities before sequencing ancient bones.

slides.heading: Our Past Is Still Being Written
slides.body: Every ancient genome decoded adds a new chapter to the human story. We are not one unbroken lineage — we are a mosaic of migrations, mergers, and lost peoples whose echoes live on inside us all.
